content.text: Negligence requires proving four elements: (1) DUTY - Did defendant owe plaintiff a duty of care? General standard: reasonable person under the circumstances. Special standards for professionals, common carriers, landowners. Cardozo view (foreseeable plaintiff) vs. Andrews view (duty to world). (2) BREACH - Did defendant fall below the standard of care? Consider custom, statutes (negligence per se), res ipsa loquitur. (3) CAUSATION - Actual cause (but-for or substantial factor) AND proximate cause (foreseeability). Intervening acts may break chain. (4) DAMAGES - Actual harm required (unlike intentional torts). Compensatory (economic + non-economic) and sometimes punitive. Don't forget affirmative defenses: contributory negligence, comparative fault, assumption of risk.
What torts might arise in estate administration?

Estate administration can involve several tort issues: (1) BREACH OF FIDUCIARY DUTY - executor/trustee failing to act in beneficiaries' best interests, self-dealing, failure to diversify investments. (2) INTENTIONAL INTERFERENCE WITH INHERITANCE - third party wrongfully causing testator to change estate plan (undue influence + causation of disinheritance). (3) PROFESSIONAL MALPRACTICE - attorney negligence in drafting, tax planning, or administration advice. (4) FRAUD/MISREPRESENTATION - inducing estate plan changes through false statements. (5) CONVERSION - wrongfully taking estate assets. (6) DEFAMATION - false statements about beneficiaries or fiduciaries. Damages may include the lost inheritance, punitive damages for intentional misconduct, and attorney fees in some jurisdictions.
